name: Ananias (from Damascus, baptized Paul)
title: The disciple who baptized Paul in Damascus
summary: Ananias was a devout disciple living in Damascus, known for his good testimony among the city's Jewish population and his faithfulness to the law. Through a vision he received a direct commission from the risen Lord to go to Straight Street and seek out Saul of Tarsus, who had been knocked to the ground and blinded on the way to Damascus. Although Ananias feared Saul's reputation as a ruthless persecutor of believers, he chose to obey the Lord's voice. When he laid hands on Saul, his sight was restored and he was filled with the Holy Spirit. Then Ananias baptized him and delivered God's calling: Saul was chosen as an instrument to carry the Lord's name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel. Ananias' courageous obedience thus became a key moment in salvation history – without his willingness to serve, the transition from persecutor Saul to apostle Paul might have looked completely different.
roles: instrument for healing and the gift of the Holy Spirit

keyEvents.title: Received a vision from the Lord
keyEvents.description: The Lord spoke to Ananias in a vision and told him to go to the house of Judas on Straight Street to find Saul of Tarsus, who was praying.

keyEvents.title: Overcame his fear through obedience
keyEvents.description: Ananias expressed his fear of Saul because of the harm he had done to the saints in Jerusalem, but the Lord assured him that Saul was a chosen instrument to carry the Lord's name before Gentiles, kings, and the people of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Laid hands on Saul – healing and baptism
keyEvents.description: Ananias entered the house, laid his hands on Saul, and said: 'Saul, brother, the Lord Jesus has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.' Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes. Saul regained his sight, got up, and was baptized.

keyEvents.title: Described as a godly man
keyEvents.description: When Paul later told the crowd in Jerusalem about his conversion, he described Ananias as a devout man who lived according to the law and had a good reputation among all the Jews in Damascus. Ananias had conveyed God's call to him to be a witness for all people.

versions.summary: Ananias was a believing disciple in Damascus who was called by the Lord to seek out the newly converted Saul (Paul). Despite fear of Saul's previous persecution of Christians, he obeyed God's call, laid hands on him, and Saul regained his sight and was baptized. His obedience was crucial for the beginning of Paul's ministry as apostle to the Gentiles.
versions.title: The Lord's Obedient Servant
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Lord's Obedient Servant' is clear, but could have been more specific and descriptive to distinguish this Ananias from other biblical figures. A title including his role in Paul's conversion would have been more informative.; [major] Ananias is described in Acts 22:12 as a 'devout man who lived according to the law' and had a good reputation among the Jews in Damascus. He also laid hands on Saul for healing and filling with the Holy Spirit. The roles should include something reflecting that he served as an instrument of healing and impartation of the Spirit, not merely 'disciple' and 'servant'.; [minor] The title 'Healed and Baptized Saul' is somewhat imprecise. The text in Acts 9:17-18 indicates that Ananias laid hands on him so that he might regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. The healing was specifically restoration of sight rather than general healing. The title is acceptable but could be clarified.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could also mention that according to Paul's own testimony (Acts 22:14-16), Ananias conveyed God's call and mission to Paul, including that he was to be a witness to all people. This further emphasizes Ananias' role.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be covered: the Hebrew origin of the name Ananias, the historical context with Damascus as an early Christian center, and the theological significance of laying on of hands.

versions.summary: Ananias was a believing disciple in Damascus, described as a godly man who lived according to the law and had a good reputation among the Jews in the city. He was called by the Lord in a vision to seek out the newly converted Saul (Paul) on Straight Street. Despite his fear of Saul's former persecution of Christians, Ananias obeyed God's call. He laid hands on Saul, who thereby regained his sight, was filled with the Holy Spirit, and was baptized. Ananias also conveyed God's call and mission to Saul—that he should be a witness to all people about what he had seen and heard. His obedience was crucial for the beginning of Paul's ministry as apostle to the Gentiles.
versions.title: The disciple who baptized Paul in Damascus

footnotes.text: The name Ananias (Greek: Ἁνανίας) comes from the Hebrew חֲנַנְיָה (Chananja), which means 'the Lord is gracious' or 'Yahweh has shown grace.' It is a very common name in the Old Testament and appears for three different individuals in the New Testament.

Damascus was one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and had a significant Jewish population in the first century. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions that there was a large Jewish colony in the city. That Christian believers were already present there so early testifies to the rapid spread of the gospel from Jerusalem.

'Straight Street' (Greek: ῥύμη Εὐθεῖα) in Damascus can be identified with the ancient main street that ran across the city from east to west. This street, known in Latin as Via Recta, still exists today as Midhat Pasha Street and is an important archaeological landmark.

Laying on of hands (Greek: ἐπιτίθημι τὰς χεῖρας) was an established practice in Jewish tradition for blessing, ordination, and the transfer of authority. In the early church, it was used in connection with healing, the imparting of the Holy Spirit, and commissioning into ministry. Ananias laying hands on Saul encompassed all these dimensions.

In rabbinic tradition, laying hands on someone (סמיכה, semikha) was linked to the transfer of authority, as when Moses laid hands on Joshua (Num 27:18–23). Ananias' action can be seen as a continuation of this tradition, where God's call and mission were conveyed through a human intermediary.
